original_interpretation: Gartner estimated that AI semiconductors (processors, high-bandwidth memory and networking components) accounted for nearly one-third of total semiconductor sales in 2025.
evidence_found: "AI semiconductors — including processors, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and networking components continued to drive unprecedented growth in the semiconductor market, accounting for nearly one-third of total sales in 2025," said Rajeev Rajput (Gartner press release, 12 Jan 2026, para 2)
notes: Preliminary Gartner figure (Q4 estimated). Gartner's April 2026 release (re-opened) revises the 2025 total to US$805.3bn but gives no revised AI share for 2025; it forecasts AI semis at ~30% of 2026 revenue, so no newer 2025 share supersedes this.

original_interpretation: Gartner estimated that high-bandwidth memory (HBM) represented 23% of the DRAM market in 2025 and surpassed US$30 billion in sales.
evidence_found: "In 2025, HBM represented 23% of the DRAM market, surpassing $30 billion in sales while AI processors exceeded $200 billion in sales." (Gartner press release, 12 Jan 2026, paragraph after Table 1)
notes: Researcher's evidence was a paraphrase; the verbatim sentence is now quoted. Preliminary-results release.

original_interpretation: Gartner's final estimate put 2024 worldwide semiconductor revenue at US$655.9 billion, up 21% from US$542.1 billion in 2023.
evidence_found: "Worldwide semiconductor revenue totaled $655.9 billion in 2024, up 21% from $542.1 billion in 2023, according to final results by Gartner"; Table 1 Total Market 655,882 (2024) vs 542,054 (2023), growth 21.0% (Gartner, 10 Apr 2025)

original_interpretation: Gartner's preliminary estimate (February 2025) put 2024 worldwide semiconductor revenue at US$626 billion, up 18.1%.
evidence_found: "Worldwide semiconductor revenue in 2024 totaled $626 billion, an increase of 18.1% from 2023, according to preliminary results by Gartner"; Table 1 Total Market 625,971 (Gartner, 3 Feb 2025)
notes: Accurate as a dated statement of the preliminary estimate. Superseded as data by Gartner's final US$655.9bn (CLM-0053); use CLM-0053 for the 2024 market size.

original_interpretation: ISIC Rev.4 class 2610 (Manufacture of electronic components and boards) groups integrated circuits, microprocessors, diodes and transistors and semiconductor wafers together with electronic capacitors, resistors, inductors, connectors, bare printed circuit boards, LCD/plasma display components, LEDs and the loading of components onto printed circuit boards.
evidence_found: 'This class includes:' - manufacture of capacitors, electronic; resistors, electronic; microprocessors; bare printed circuit boards; electronic connectors; integrated circuits (analog, digital or hybrid); diodes, transistors and related discrete devices; inductors; dice or wafers, semiconductor; display components (plasma, polymer, LCD); light emitting diodes (LED); loading of components onto printed circuit boards (UNSD ISIC Rev.4 class 2610, explanatory note)
notes: web_extract returned only the page header; full text read in browser.

original_interpretation: ISIC Rev.4 class 2610 excludes manufacture of computer and television displays and printing of smart cards; complete equipment is classified elsewhere.
evidence_found: 'This class excludes:' - "printing of smart cards, see 1811"; "manufacture of computer and television displays, see 2620, 2640"; "manufacture of complete equipment is classified elsewhere based on complete equipment classification" (UNSD ISIC Rev.4 2610)

original_interpretation: The Canadian NAICS 2022 industry 334410 (Semiconductor and other electronic component manufacturing) lists as illustrative examples electronic capacitors, integrated microcircuits, solar cells, printed circuit laminates, semiconductor wafers, transistors and loaded computer boards.
evidence_found: 334410 illustrative examples include: "capacitors, electronic, fixed and variable, manufacturing"; "integrated microcircuits, manufacturing"; "loaded computer boards, manufacturing"; "printed circuit laminates, manufacturing"; "semiconductor devices (e.g., wafers), manufacturing"; "solar cells, manufacturing"; "transistors, manufacturing" (Statistics Canada, NAICS Canada 2022 v1.0, 334410)
notes: This is the Canadian NAICS (334410 is a Canadian/MEX 6-digit industry); the US 6-digit split differs (334412-334419).

original_interpretation: The Harmonized System (Chapter 85, Note 12) defines semiconductor devices as devices whose operation depends on variations in resistivity on the application of an electric field, or semiconductor-based transducers.
evidence_found: 12.(a)(i) "Semiconductor devices" are semiconductor devices the operation of which depends on variations in resistivity on the application of an electric field or semiconductor-based transducers. (Schedule B 2022, Chapter 85, Note 12)
notes: Schedule B reproduces the HS 2022 legal note; read in browser (web_extract returned only navigation).

original_interpretation: For customs purposes (HS heading 8542), electronic integrated circuits comprise monolithic, hybrid, multichip and multi-component integrated circuits (MCOs).
evidence_found: 12.(b) "Electronic integrated circuits" are: (i) Monolithic integrated circuits ... (ii) Hybrid integrated circuits ... (iii) Multichip integrated circuits ... (iv) Multi-component integrated circuits (MCOs) ... (Schedule B 2022, Chapter 85, Note 12(b))

original_interpretation: The Harmonized System classifies light-emitting diodes as semiconductor devices.
evidence_found: 12.(a)(ii) "Light-emitting diodes (LED)" are semiconductor devices based on semiconductor materials which convert electrical energy into visible, infra-red or ultra-violet rays (Schedule B 2022, Chapter 85, Note 12)

original_interpretation: The U.S. CHIPS statute defines eligible 'covered entities' by facilities for fabrication, assembly, testing, advanced packaging, production or R&D of semiconductors, materials used to manufacture semiconductors, or semiconductor manufacturing equipment, so U.S. policy treats equipment and materials as part of the semiconductor industry.
evidence_found: (2) "covered entity" means a nonprofit entity, a private entity, a consortium ... with a demonstrated ability to substantially finance, construct, expand, or modernize a facility relating to fabrication, assembly, testing, advanced packaging, production, or research and development of semiconductors, materials used to manufacture semiconductors, or semiconductor manufacturing equipment. (15 U.S.C. 4651(2))
correction: The statutory definition is verified, but it defines covered entities by their ability to finance/build such facilities (not 'by facilities'), and it only makes materials and equipment facilities eligible for CHIPS incentives; the statute does not say these are 'part of the semiconductor industry' - that is our interpretation. See superseding claim.
notes: Para (2) text read on uscode.house.gov (first extract); the site then showed a maintenance page, so LII reproduction used to confirm full text.

original_interpretation: The U.S. CHIPS statute does not itself define 'semiconductor' or 'mature technology node'; both have the meaning given by the Secretary of Commerce.
evidence_found: "(10) The term 'mature technology node' has the meaning given the term by the Secretary." ... "(13) The term 'semiconductor' has the meaning given that term by the Secretary."; "(12) The term 'Secretary' means the Secretary of Commerce." (15 U.S.C. 4651, LII reproduction)
notes: uscode.house.gov returned truncated text then a maintenance page; paras (10), (12), (13) read on the LII reproduction of the same section (Pub. L. 117-167 text).

original_interpretation: U.S. Commerce regulations define a semiconductor as an integrated electronic device or system most commonly manufactured using materials such as silicon, silicon carbide or III-V compounds.
evidence_found: "Semiconductor means an integrated electronic device or system most commonly manufactured using materials such as, but not limited to, silicon, silicon carbide, or III-V compounds, and processes such as, but not limited to, lithography, deposition, and etching." (15 CFR 231.115, eCFR as of 2026-09-01)
notes: eCFR HTML page (SRC-0019) is CAPTCHA-gated; read the official eCFR API text and the LII copy. Definition also lists analog/digital, power electronics and photonics.

original_interpretation: U.S. Commerce regulations define semiconductor manufacturing as three stages: wafer production, semiconductor fabrication and semiconductor packaging.
evidence_found: "Semiconductor manufacturing means semiconductor wafer production, semiconductor fabrication or semiconductor packaging." (15 CFR 231.116, eCFR as of 2026-09-01)

original_interpretation: U.S. CHIPS guardrail regulations define 'legacy' fabrication as digital/analog logic at the 28-nanometer generation or older, DRAM with half-pitch above 18 nm, or NAND flash with fewer than 128 layers; legacy wafer production covers silicon wafers of 200 mm or smaller.
evidence_found: 231.107(a): wafer facility - "A silicon wafer measuring 8 inches (or 200 millimeters) or smaller" or compound wafer 6 inches or smaller; fabrication - logic "of the 28-nanometer generation or older", memory "half-pitch greater than 18 nanometers for ... DRAM or less than 128 layers for ... NAND flash" (15 CFR 231.107, eCFR as of 2026-09-01)
notes: Memory limb also excludes emerging memory technologies; paragraph (a)(2)(iii) lets the Secretary designate further legacy chips by notice.

original_interpretation: Under U.S. CHIPS guardrail regulations, chips using post-planar transistor architectures (such as FinFET or gate-all-around) or advanced 3D integration packaging are not legacy semiconductors.
evidence_found: 231.107(b): "the following are not legacy semiconductors: (1) Semiconductors critical to national security ... (2) A semiconductor with a post-planar transistor architecture (such as ... FinFET or gate all around ...); and (3) A semiconductor utilizing advanced three-dimensional (3D) integration packaging" (15 CFR 231.107, eCFR as of 2026-09-01)

original_interpretation: SEMI reported worldwide semiconductor manufacturing equipment sales of US$135.1 billion in 2025, up 15% from US$117.1 billion in 2024.
evidence_found: "Worldwide sales of semiconductor manufacturing equipment increased 15% to $135.1 billion in 2025 from $117.1 billion in 2024" (SEMI press release, Milpitas, 7 Apr 2026, para 1)

original_interpretation: SEMI's equipment statistics are compiled from data submitted by members of SEMI and the Semiconductor Equipment Association of Japan (SEAJ), covering seven regions and over 22 market segments.
evidence_found: "Compiled from data submitted by members of SEMI and the Semiconductor Equipment Association of Japan (SEAJ), the WWSEMS report is a summary of the monthly billings figures"; WWSEMS is "a detailed report of semiconductor equipment billings for seven regions and more than 22 market segments" (SEMI, 7 Apr 2026)

original_interpretation: SEMI segments equipment into front-end (wafer processing and other front-end) and back-end (test, and assembly and packaging); in 2025 test equipment grew 55% and assembly and packaging equipment 21%.
evidence_found: "wafer processing equipment sales increasing 12% and other front-end segments rising 13%"; "Test equipment billings surged 55% year-over-year ... while assembly and packaging equipment sales rose 21%" (SEMI, 7 Apr 2026, paras 2-3)

original_interpretation: China was the largest regional market for semiconductor equipment in 2025 at US$49.3 billion.
evidence_found: "In 2025, spending in China remained near record levels at $49.3 billion, down just 0.5% from the prior year"; Taiwan $31.5bn, Korea $25.8bn, North America $10.9bn, Japan $9.5bn (SEMI, 7 Apr 2026, regional section)
notes: China is the largest of the seven SEMI regions listed. The release text repeats the China paragraph twice (publisher error), no conflict.

original_interpretation: SEMI reported 2025 semiconductor materials revenue of US$73.2 billion (+6.8%), of which wafer fabrication materials were US$45.8 billion and packaging materials US$27.4 billion.
evidence_found: "Global semiconductor materials market revenue increased 6.8% year-over-year to $73.2 billion in 2025"; "Wafer fabrication materials revenue increased 5.4% to $45.8 billion"; "Packaging materials revenue grew 9.3% to $27.4 billion in 2025" (SEMI, 12 May 2026)

original_interpretation: The ESD Alliance reported electronic system design (EDA plus semiconductor IP and services) revenue of US$5.47 billion in Q4 2025, up 10.3% year over year.
evidence_found: "Electronic System Design (ESD) industry revenue increased 10.3% to $5,466.3 million in the fourth quarter of 2025 from the $4,955.2 million registered in the fourth quarter of 2024" (ESD Alliance / SEMI, 13 Apr 2026)
notes: Source publication date was 'unknown'; release is dated 13 Apr 2026 (patched in updates.jsonl). Totals include PCB/MCM design tools and services, not only chip design.

original_interpretation: Semiconductor IP was the largest ESD Alliance category in Q4 2025 at US$2.08 billion (+18.3%).
evidence_found: "Semiconductor Intellectual Property (SIP) revenue increased 18.3% to $2,083.2 million" vs CAE $1,887.4m, IC Physical Design & Verification $777.2m, PCB & MCM $484.6m, Services $233.9m (ESD Alliance, 13 Apr 2026)

original_interpretation: TSMC defines a 'Foundry 2.0' market that adds packaging, testing, mask-making and others, and all non-memory IDM manufacturing, to traditional foundry.
evidence_found: "we would like to expand our original definition of foundry industry to Foundry 2.0, which also includes packaging, testing, mask-making, and others, and all IDM excluding memory manufacturing." (C.C. Wei, TSMC 2Q24 call, 18 Jul 2024, p. 4)
notes: Passage is on p. 4 of the IR transcript, not p. 3. In Jan 2026 TSMC restated it as 'all logic wafer manufacturing, packaging, testing, mask-making and others' (consistent).

original_interpretation: TSMC stated the foundry industry was close to US$250 billion in 2023 under its Foundry 2.0 definition versus US$115 billion under the previous definition.
evidence_found: "Under this new definition, the size of the foundry industry was close to USD250 billion in 2023 as compared to USD115 billion under the previous definition." (C.C. Wei, TSMC 2Q24 call, p. 4)

original_interpretation: TSMC stated its share of the foundry industry under the Foundry 2.0 definition was 28% in 2023.
evidence_found: "TSMC's share of the foundry industry under our new definition was 28% in 2023." (C.C. Wei, TSMC 2Q24 call, p. 4)

original_interpretation: TSMC's 2025 net revenue was US$122.42 billion (NT$3,809.05 billion).
evidence_found: "Net revenue was NT$3,809.05 billion, representing a 31.6% increase from 2024. In US dollar terms, net revenue increased 35.9% to US$122.42 billion in 2025." (TSMC 4Q25 Management Report, 15 Jan 2026, p. 1)

original_interpretation: In 2025, TSMC's 3nm, 5nm and 7nm processes accounted for 24%, 36% and 14% of its wafer revenue; 'advanced technologies' (7nm and below) were 74%.
evidence_found: "On a full year basis, 3nm contribution reached 24% of total wafer revenue in 2025 while 5nm and 7nm process technology contributed 36% and 14% respectively. Advanced technologies (7nm and below) accounted for 74% of total wafer revenue, up from 69% in 2024." (TSMC 4Q25 Management Report, p. 2)

original_interpretation: TSMC segments revenue by platform; in 2025 high-performance computing was 58%, smartphone 29%, IoT 5%, automotive 5% and digital consumer electronics 1%.
evidence_found: Net Revenue by Platform, 2025: High Performance Computing 58%, Smartphone 29%, Internet of Things 5%, Automotive 5%, Digital Consumer Electronics 1%, Others 2% (TSMC 4Q25 Management Report, p. 1 table)

original_interpretation: TSMC estimated the Foundry 2.0 industry (all logic wafer manufacturing, packaging, testing, mask-making and others) grew 16% in 2025 and forecast 14% growth in 2026.
evidence_found: "Concluding 2025, the foundry 2.0 industry, which we define as all logic wafer manufacturing, packaging, testing, mask-making and others, increased 16% year over year." ... "We forecast the foundry 2.0 industry to grow 14% year over year in 2026, supported by robust AI related demand." (C.C. Wei, TSMC 4Q25 call, 15 Jan 2026)
notes: The 14% is a January 2026 forecast. The 1Q26 call prepared remarks (re-opened) do not update it; the 2Q26 IR transcript could not be read in full (extract truncated, browser 403), so a mid-year revision cannot be ruled out. TSMC raised its own 2026 growth guidance to 'slightly above 40%' in July 2026.

original_interpretation: In the U.S. International Trade Administration's 2016 semiconductor report, company market-share data were based on the headquarters of the seller, with foundry output not included and fabless companies included.
evidence_found: Figure 1 'Global Market Share of Semiconductor Production, 2015' source line: "Source: SIA/World Semiconductor Trade Statistics (WSTS)/IHS/PwC/IC Insights Share based on headquarters of seller: Foundry output not included, fabless included." (ITA 2016 Top Markets Report, Executive Summary, p. 1)
notes: legacy.trade.gov failed (TLS error / timeout); read the Wayback Machine capture (2023-09-27) of the same PDF.

original_interpretation: The U.S. ITA noted that overseas packaging, final assembly and transshipments skew semiconductor import and export data, making trade statistics a poor measure of where chips are made or consumed.
evidence_found: "It was difficult in the case of semiconductors, however, due to overseas packaging and final assembly of semiconductors and transshipments skewing the import and export data." (ITA 2016 Top Markets Report, Executive Summary, Methodology)
correction: ITA says this skewing made it difficult to rank export markets for semiconductors (unlike equipment), and that it then used WSTS regional market data instead. It does not say trade statistics are a poor measure of where chips are made or consumed; that is our extension. See superseding claim.

original_interpretation: Process-node names such as '14 nm' or '22 nm' no longer correspond to any specific physical dimension on the chip.
evidence_found: "But the names no longer match the size of any specific chip dimension. ... 'But I'm the first to admit that I can't point to the one dimension that's 32 nm or 22 nm or 14 nm. Some dimensions are smaller than the stated node name, and others are larger.'" (Mark Bohr, Intel, in IEEE Spectrum, 'The Status of Moore's Law: It's Complicated', 2013)
notes: Source is from 2013 but the point (node names are labels, not a measured feature) has only become more true since; IEEE Spectrum is specialist press (tier 2).

original_interpretation: Samsung describes the semiconductor ecosystem as made up of integrated device manufacturers (IDMs), fabless designers, foundries, design houses, OSATs (outsourced assembly and test) and IP companies.
evidence_found: Sections: "1) Integrated Device Manufacturer (IDM)" ("corporations that handles all processes in manufacturing semiconductors"), "2) IP (Intellectual Property) Companies", "3) Fabless", "4) Design House", "5) Foundry", "6) OSAT" ("takes clients in to package and test semiconductors") (Samsung Semiconductor tech blog)
notes: Correctly typed as reported_claim (a company's explainer).

original_interpretation: TrendForce estimated revenue of the top 10 pure foundry-service providers at about US$46.3 billion in 4Q25, with TSMC holding a 70.4% share.
evidence_found: "these factors pushed the combined revenue of the world's top ten foundries up 2.6% QoQ to nearly US$46.3 billion in 4Q25"; TSMC revenue "$33.7 billion, which allowed TSMC to maintain its leading position with a 70.4% market share"; "Samsung Foundry (excluding System LSI)" (TrendForce, 12 Mar 2026)
correction: TrendForce ranks the 'top ten foundries', not 'pure foundry-service providers': Samsung Foundry (a division of IDM Samsung) is No. 2. Figures (US$46.3bn; TSMC 70.4%) are correct. See superseding claim.
notes: Period-specific (4Q25); later quarterly rankings exist but do not make this one wrong. TrendForce also gives ~US$169.5bn for the top ten in full-year 2025.

original_interpretation: SIA and BCG use 'DAO' to group discretes, analog, and optoelectronics and sensors, and segment wafer-fab capacity into DRAM, NAND, logic by node (<10nm, 10-22nm, 28nm and above) and DAO.
evidence_found: Slide 6 footnote: "1. Discretes, analog, and optoelectronics & sensors"; capacity chart rows: "DRAM", "NAND", "Logic: <10 nm", "Logic: 10-22 nm", "Logic: 28 nm+", "DAO1", "Total" (SIA/BCG 'Emerging Resilience in the Semiconductor Supply Chain' briefing deck, slide 6)
notes: Deck cover says 'JUNE 2024 Briefing deck' (source date patched from 2024-05). Read from the PDF text layer, not a chart image.

original_interpretation: SIA and BCG found more than 50 points across the semiconductor value chain where one region holds more than 65% of global market share.
evidence_found: "There are more than 50 points across the value chain where one region holds more than 65% of the global market share" (SIA/BCG 'Strengthening the Global Semiconductor Supply Chain in an Uncertain Era' 2-page summary, Mar 2021, right column)
notes: PDF uses a substituted font; text decoded from the text layer. A 2021 finding; the 2024 SIA/BCG deck still cites '50+ Chokepoints'.

original_interpretation: Pure-play foundry wafer revenue is unlikely to be counted as a separate population in the WSTS headline market, because WSTS reporting is by companies selling chips under their own trade name; chips made by foundries are counted when sold by their (fabless) customers.
evidence_found: WSTS: "A company that at least designs and sells semiconductor products under its own trade name may become WSTS member." WSTS foundry page: "Semiconductor Manufacturers who cannot join WSTS as Member for whatever reason (e.g. acting as a foundry) may enter a subscription with a foundry membership". ITA: "Foundry output not included, fabless included."
notes: Reasoning follows and is now stronger: WSTS's own foundry-subscription page says foundries cannot be regular (reporting) members. Still an inference about WSTS methodology; WSTS does not state foundry treatment of its totals in so many words.

original_interpretation: Official industrial classifications (ISIC 2610, NAICS 334410) define a wider population than the industry-body 'semiconductor market': they bundle semiconductors with passive components, printed circuit boards and (in NAICS) solar cells, so official production and employment statistics are not directly comparable with WSTS sales figures.
evidence_found: Checked the premises: ISIC 2610 includes electronic capacitors, resistors, connectors, bare PCBs, LCD display components and board loading (SRC-0015); NAICS Canada 334410 includes capacitors, solar cells, printed circuit laminates and loaded computer boards (SRC-0016).
notes: Reasoning follows from verified CLM-0017/CLM-0019 plus WSTS display exclusion (CLM-0015, not re-checked here). WSTS solar-cell treatment remains unknown (CLM-0016).

original_interpretation: Two incompatible regional conventions coexist: WSTS regional market data describe where chips are sold (e.g. Americas US$256.5bn in 2025), while 'industry share' figures attribute sales to the seller's headquarters country (e.g. U.S.-HQ firms 50.4% of global sales in 2024).
evidence_found: WSTS Spring 2026 table: "Americas 256,476" (US$M, 2025). SIA 2025 report: "U.S. headquartered companies reaching sales of $318 billion, accounting for 50.4% of global sales revenue"; chart 'GLOBAL MARKET SHARE BY COMPANY HQ'. ITA: "Share based on headquarters of seller".
notes: Both example figures confirmed in the primary documents. Reasoning holds; WSTS's regional attribution basis (ship-to vs bill-to) is still not public (CLM-0080).

original_interpretation: The headline 'semiconductor market' (~US$0.8 trillion in 2025) counts only chip sales; equipment (US$135bn), materials (US$73bn) and EDA/IP (~US$5.5bn per quarter) are measured by different bodies as separate markets and are inputs to, not part of, that figure.
evidence_found: WSTS 2025 total "795,640" US$M (SRC-0001); SEMI equipment "$135.1 billion in 2025" (SRC-0020); SEMI materials "$73.2 billion in 2025" (SRC-0021); ESD Alliance Q4 2025 "$5,466.3 million" (SRC-0022).
correction: All four figures check out, and they are separate from the chip-sales market. But they are not measured by 'different bodies' in each case: equipment and materials both come from SEMI, and the ESD Alliance is a SEMI Technology Community. EDA/IP revenue also includes PCB/MCM design tools and services, not only chip design.
notes: The double-counting point holds for materials and EDA/IP. Equipment is capital spending, so it reaches chip prices only through depreciation.
